'''Naomi Shauna Ginsberg''' (born 1979) is a Canadian electrical engineer and scientist. She is currently a professor of chemistry and physics at the [[University of California]], [[University of California, Berkeley|Berkeley.]]

==Life and education==
Ginsberg was born in [[Halifax (former city)|Halifax, Nova Scotia]]. She earned her B.Sc. in engineering at the [[University of Toronto]] in 2000, and completed her PhD in physics at [[Harvard]].

Her initial interest was biomedicine, but she graduated with an electrical engineering focus, and an emphasis on physics and optics.  Accepted into Harvard, and while working in the research group of physics professor [[Lene Hau]], Ginsberg studied [[Bose–Einstein condensate|Bose–Einstein condensates]], ultracold clouds of atoms that exist at temperatures just a few billionths of a degree above [[absolute zero]].

After being awarded her PhD for her thesis entitled "Manipulations with spatially compressed slow light pulses in Bose–Einstein condensates" with [[Lene Hau]] as her thesis advisor,<ref>{{cite web |date=2012-09-26 |title=Harvard Physics Department - PhD Theses: 2000 to present |url=http://www.physics.harvard.edu/academics/phds.html#y2007 |access-date=2013-01-26 |publisher=Physics.harvard.edu |archive-date=2013-07-24 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130724053528/http://www.physics.harvard.edu/academics/phds.html#y2007 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Ginsberg chose to change direction and include other interests, moving to Berkeley to begin her postdoctoral research in 2007 with [[Graham Fleming]] as her advisor. She held a [[Glenn T. Seaborg]] Postdoctoral Fellowship at [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]], until her appointment as an assistant professor in the chemistry department at UC Berkeley in 2010.

==Work==
In a series of experiments the Hau Group at Harvard (which included Ginsberg) halted and stored a light signal in a condensate of sodium atoms, then transferred the signal into a second sodium cloud 160&nbsp;[[μm]] away. The [[American Institute of Physics]] listed this feat as #1 in its Top Ten discoveries of 2007.<ref name="welcome2">{{cite web |date=2011-01-18 |title=UC Berkeley, College of Chemistry - News and Publications - Chemistry welcomes Naomi Ginsberg: Bringing photosynthesis to light |url=http://chemistry.berkeley.edu/publications/news/2011/chemistry_welcomes_naomi_ginsberg.php |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402105513/http://chemistry.berkeley.edu/publications/news/2011/chemistry_welcomes_naomi_ginsberg.php |archive-date=2015-04-02 |access-date=2013-01-26 |publisher=Chemistry.berkeley.edu}}</ref>

Ginsberg was the lead author on the paper "Coherent control of optical information with [[matter wave]] dynamics", that appeared on the cover of Nature <ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ginsberg |first1=N. S. |last2=Garner |first2=S. R. |last3=Hau |first3=L. V. |year=2007 |title=Coherent control of optical information with matter wave dynamics : Abstract |url=http://nrs.harvard.edu/urn-3:HUL.InstRepos:3636963 |journal=Nature |volume=445 |issue=7128 |pages=623–626 |doi=10.1038/nature05493 |pmid=17287804 |s2cid=4324343}}</ref> in February of that year.<ref name="welcome2" />

She now leads the Ginsberg Group, whose research objective is "to spatially resolve the complex dynamics of nanoscale processes such as [[photosynthetic]] light harvesting."<ref>{{cite web |title=Research - Ginsberg Group |url=http://www.cchem.berkeley.edu/nsggrp/ |access-date=2013-01-26 |publisher=UC Berkeley}}</ref> Her current work is centered on "pushing the limits of spatially resolved spectroscopy and time resolved microscopy in multiple modalities", in order to try to answer fundamental and challenging questions that span chemistry, physics, and biology. Ginsberg's group uses multiple approaches, including [[Ultrafast laser spectroscopy|ultrafast spectroscopy]], [[Optical microscope|light microscopy]], and [[Cathodoluminescence microscope|cathodoluminescence electron microscopy]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Interdisciplinary |url=http://www.physics.berkeley.edu/research/faculty/ginsberg.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130112221338/http://www.physics.berkeley.edu/research/faculty/ginsberg.html |archive-date=2013-01-12 |access-date=2013-01-25 |website=berkeley.edu}}</ref>

==Awards==
In 2011, Ginsberg was awarded the [[David and Lucile Packard Foundation]] Fellowship for Science and Engineering.

In 2012, Her research attracted support from the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency [[DARPA]] in the form of a Young Faculty Award for her work in "Predictive Materials Science; "Beneath the Bulk: Domain-Specific Efficiency and Degradation in Organic Photovoltaic Thin Films""<ref>{{cite web |title=2012 Young Faculty Award Recipients |url=http://www.darpa.mil/opportunities/universities/young_faculty_award_recipients_2012.aspx |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130221202811/http://www.darpa.mil/Opportunities/Universities/Young_Faculty_Award_Recipients_2012.aspx |archive-date=2013-02-21 |access-date=2013-01-26 |publisher=Darpa.mil}}</ref>

Ginsberg currently holds The Cupola Era Endowed Chair in the college of chemistry, and is a faculty scientist in the physical biosciences division at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

In 2015, Ginsberg was awarded a [[Sloan Research Fellow|Sloan Research Fellowship]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Sloan Fellowships Give Research Boost to Nine Young Faculty |url=http://newscenter.berkeley.edu/2015/02/23/sloan-fellowships-give-research-boost-to-nine-young-faculty-members/ |access-date=Mar 11, 2015 |location=[[University of California, Berkeley]]}}</ref>

In 2021, Ginsberg was named a [[Fellow of the American Physical Society]] (APS), after a nomination from the APS Division of Chemical Physics, "for the innovative development of spatiotemporally resolved imaging and spectroscopy methods, and for their use in elucidating energy transport in hierarchical and heterogeneous materials, as well as in the formation and transformation of said materials".<ref>{{cite web |title=Fellows nominated in 2021 by the Division of Chemical Physics |url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=2021&unit_id=DCP&institution= |access-date=2021-10-22 |work=APS Fellows archive |publisher=American Physical Society}}</ref>

In 2022, Ginsberg was awarded the Carol D. Soc Distinguished Graduate Student Mentoring Award for Later-Career Faculty.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Award Recipients {{!}} Graduate Mentoring Awards |url=https://mentoringawards.berkeley.edu/award-recipients/ |access-date=2026-09-24 |website=mentoringawards.berkeley.edu}}</ref>
